articles.title: Why Does Popcorn Pop?
articles.dek: A tiny hard seed turns into a big white snack. How does it happen?
paras: Do you like eating popcorn at the cinema? It is light, warm and crunchy. But every piece starts as a small, hard yellow seed. How does a tiny seed turn into a big white snack? Let's find out step by step.

First, popcorn is a special kind of corn. Every seed, or kernel, has a very hard skin. Inside the skin, there is soft starch and a little water. About fourteen percent of the kernel is water. That small drop of water is the secret.

Next, you heat the kernels. When they get hot, the water inside turns into steam. Steam needs a lot of space, but it can't get out through the hard skin. So the pressure inside the kernel grows and grows.

At about 180 degrees Celsius, the skin can't hold the steam any more. Suddenly it breaks open with a loud pop! The soft starch comes out and turns into a white foam. It cools very quickly and becomes crunchy. A popped kernel can be twenty to fifty times bigger than before!

Why do some kernels stay hard at the bottom of the bowl? Usually they are too dry. With too little water, there isn't enough steam to break the skin. That is why you shouldn't keep popcorn kernels in a warm, dry place. You should keep them in a closed box.

Do you want to make popcorn at home? You should always ask an adult for help, because hot oil is dangerous. You should put a lid on the pan, or the popcorn will fly everywhere! And you shouldn't eat the hard kernels, because they can hurt your teeth.

People have enjoyed popcorn for a very long time. Scientists found very old popcorn in Peru, in South America. It is more than six thousand years old! So next time you hear that pop, remember the tiny drop of water inside.

articles.title: Our Science Fair Plans
articles.dek: Lucas and Mia are getting ready for a big day at school.
paras: Lucas and Mia are in Year 8 at Riverside School. Next Friday, their school is having a science fair. Every pair of students must show a project. Read their emails.

Hi Mia, Good news! Mr Okafor said yes to our idea. We're going to make a small water filter from a plastic bottle, sand and stones. Then we're going to clean some dirty water from the river. I think the visitors are going to love it! After the fair, we're going to give the filter to our science class.

I've got a very busy week. I'm playing football on Tuesday afternoon, and I'm visiting my grandma on Wednesday. Can we meet on Thursday after school? We need to practise our talk. It's only five minutes long, but I don't want to forget anything. Lucas
Hi Lucas, That's great news! Thursday is fine for me. I'm not doing anything after school that day. We can meet in the science room at four o'clock. Mr Okafor is staying late, so he can help us.

I'm going to buy the sand at the garden shop tomorrow. My dad is driving me there after lunch. Can you bring two big bottles? My family doesn't buy drinks in plastic bottles any more. Also, I'm not going to speak first in our talk. I'm too nervous! Can you start? Love, Mia
Hi Mia, No problem. I'm going to start the talk, and you can show the water filter. My mum is coming to the fair too. She's taking photos for the school website. See you on Thursday! Lucas

articles.title: Amira's Muddy Race
articles.dek: Amira hates running. Can she finish a five-kilometre race?
paras: Amira didn't like running. She was good at swimming, but running was hard for her. So she was worried when Ms Clark, her PE teacher, put her name on the list for the school cross-country race.

"I can't do it," Amira said to her friend Daniel. "The race is five kilometres. I'll be the last. Everyone will laugh at me." Daniel smiled. "No, they won't. And I'll help you. I'll run with you every morning before school."

So for three weeks, Amira and Daniel ran in the park at seven o'clock. At first, Amira stopped every few minutes. Her legs hurt, and she felt tired. But slowly she got stronger. By the third week, she could run without stopping.
On the morning of the race, it was cold and wet. Amira looked at the dark sky. "It will rain," she said. "The field will be muddy. I'll fall over!" "Then you'll get up again," Daniel laughed.

The race started. Soon the rain came, and the ground got very muddy. Amira slipped once, but she got up quickly and ran on. Some fast runners were far in front of her. She didn't stop. She thought about the cold mornings in the park. "I won't stop now," she said to herself.

Amira wasn't the first, but she wasn't the last. She finished in twenty-third place out of forty runners. Her clothes were brown with mud, but she was smiling. "I knew you could do it," said Daniel. Amira laughed. "Next year, I'll be faster. Maybe I'll beat you!"
